description: We are the Hubble Bros, a passionate team of technology enthusiasts driven by innovation, and space exploration. Our interests include programming, artificial intelligence, engineering, and scientific research. We combine technical skills, problem-solving, and teamwork to develop impactful solutions and push the boundaries of what is possible. Our team is currently complete. However, we are always open to networking.
summary:
M.E.V.A. (Mars Exploration and Virtual Adventure) is an educational web platform that transforms NASA and USGS Mars data into an interactive mission-planning and 3D exploration experience. Addressing the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge, it connects layered maps, rover traverses, and terrain models to help users explore selected areas of Jezero and Gale craters.

Users choose scientific objectives, prepare their crew and equipment, compare routes, and assess daylight constraints, resource requirements, and illustrative budgets before beginning a simulated extravehicular activity. During exploration, a heads-up display tracks time, distance, life-support resources, and radiation estimates based on a historical reference. Inspectable targets introduce rover discoveries involving ancient water, sedimentary environments, potential biosignatures, and boxwork formations.

MEVA brings otherwise dispersed scientific information into a connected experience designed for students, educators, and curious explorers. By explicitly distinguishing published observations, derived calculations, simulations, and hypothetical scenarios, it encourages scientific literacy and informed decision-making while making the challenges of human exploration on Mars easier to understand.
details:
1. EXPLORE THE MEVA PROJECT ↗

Explore the MEVA website for the full project presentation, supporting articles, scientific data sources, and a step-by-step tutorial:

Visit MEVA — Mars Exploration and Virtual Adventure

What MEVA Does

M.E.V.A. — Mars Exploration and Virtual Adventure is an educational web platform that connects Mars mission planning with interactive maps and first-person 3D exploration. Developed for the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge, it helps users understand how scientific objectives, terrain, equipment, daylight, and limited resources influence a hypothetical astronaut expedition.

Mars exploration data are distributed across different scientific portals and mission archives. MEVA brings selected information into a connected experience: users prepare an expedition, examine its requirements, explore the terrain, and review the consequences of their decisions.

Its main features include:

  • Interactive planetary maps: Explore Jezero and Gale craters using orbital imagery, elevation layers, geological context, and recorded rover traverses. (Sources include NASA/JPL Mars Trek, USGS planetary mapping products, HiRISE terrain models, and Perseverance and Curiosity mission data.)
  • Science-driven exploration: Choose objectives related to potential signs of ancient life, ancient water and sediments, or boxwork formations. Explore contextualized targets and inspect illustrative geological objects linked to documented rover investigations. (Sources include NASA/JPL science reports, mission imagery, and Curiosity campaign updates.)
  • Mission preparation: Select crew size, life-support provisions, scientific tools, mobility, and habitat concepts. Review how these choices affect the mission manifest and modeled resource requirements. (Scientific context includes NASA spacesuit, environmental control, and habitat research.)
  • Route assessment: Compare curated routes using distance, sampled slopes, estimated duration, resource reserves, and daylight constraints. (Inputs include rover waypoints, elevation data, historical MEDA/REMS weather records, and NASA GISS time conventions.)
  • 3D EVA simulation: Experience a simulated extravehicular activity with route guidance, inspectable targets, a mission manifest, and a heads-up display showing time, distance, resources, and radiation context.
  • Transparent budget exploration: Examine itemized hypothetical allowances, quantities, total cost, and average cost per crew member. (Published NASA program and contract figures provide context; the resulting allocations are educational assumptions rather than verified Mars equipment prices.)

Throughout the experience, MEVA identifies information as published, derived, simulated, or hypothetical, helping users understand both the evidence and its limitations.


How It Works

  1. Choose your destination.
    Select Jezero Crater or Gale Crater. Each destination offers relevant scientific objectives and available route scenarios.
  2. Prepare the mission.
    Review essential systems, including pressure protection, oxygen, carbon dioxide removal, cooling, power, communications, and emergency preparation.
  3. Define your scientific objective.
    Choose what you want to investigate, such as potential biosignatures, evidence of ancient water, sedimentary environments, or boxwork formations. Available objectives match the selected destination.
  4. Configure the crew and equipment.
    Select crew size, surface mobility, scientific tools, and a habitat concept. Personal equipment allowances scale with crew size, while shared provisions are counted once per mission.
  5. Choose a daylight departure window.
    Use the available historical environmental records to assess departure and return timing. This step checks daylight constraints; it does not identify a radiation-safe hour or predict solar events.
  6. Review the plan and explore the map.
    Examine the itemized budget, route characteristics, resource estimates, and warnings. Adjust selections when the scenario does not satisfy the planner’s requirements.
  7. Begin the 3D exploration.
    Follow route indicators, approach scientific targets, inspect objects, and monitor the HUD. Pause to review your manifest or adjust exploration speed, with movement, simulated time, and consumption remaining synchronized.
  8. Analyze your EVA.
    Review distance traveled, elapsed time, resources consumed, remaining reserves, and scientific targets visited. Use the results to reconsider your preparation and compare alternative scenarios.

Benefits and Goals

  • Make planetary science easier to understand: Connect maps and scientific reports to places users can explore and investigate.
  • Encourage informed decisions: Show how route length, terrain, carried equipment, and investigation time interact with limited resources.
  • Strengthen scientific literacy: Explain why evidence of ancient water does not establish a present water supply, and why a potential biosignature does not confirm life.
  • Support interdisciplinary learning: Bring together planetary geology, geography, mathematics, computing, engineering, and economic reasoning.
  • Create opportunities for classroom exploration: Provide students, educators, and curious visitors with scenarios that can support discussion and guided activities.
  • Promote transparent modeling: Make assumptions and source limitations visible so users can distinguish an observation from a simulated outcome.

MEVA’s intended impact is to make the challenges of Mars exploration more understandable and engaging. Its educational effectiveness and accessibility across different audiences remain priorities for future evaluation.

Technologies and Development

The mission planner and simulator use HTML, CSS, and JavaScript modules, with selected simulator components authored in TypeScript. Leaflet provides the interactive mapping interface, while Three.js and WebGL render the 3D environment. Python scripts prepare terrain and imagery, with Pillow supporting texture processing. JSON and GeoJSON organize mission and geographic data, and Node.js supports automated testing.

The application runs in a browser without a dedicated application backend or specialized simulation hardware. The 3D experience is designed primarily for a desktop browser with WebGL, keyboard, and mouse support.

Creativity and Design Considerations

MEVA connects preparation, geography, exploration, and reflection in one workflow. A scientific objective guides the destination and route; equipment choices appear in the mission manifest; exploration consumes modeled resources; and the final analysis helps users interpret their decisions.

Development considered terrain resolution, data coverage, historical weather, crew quantities, interface clarity, browser performance, and consistency between planning and simulation. Scientific integrity also shaped the design: procedural rocks and habitat structures are illustrative, radiation uses a historical reference rather than local live measurements, and financial allocations remain explicitly hypothetical.

This approach gives users an engaging way to explore Mars while keeping the underlying evidence and assumptions visible.
